definition.text: A way of buying or selling something by inviting bids and then dealing with the highest (or, when buying, the lowest) bidder.

facts.text: The open ascending-price auction, where each bid must beat the one before, is probably the most common kind and has a long history.
Auctions are used to trade antiques, livestock, radio spectrum, used cars, real estate, online advertising and emission permits, among much else.
Each year the US EPA auctions about 250,000 allowances, each letting its owner emit one ton of sulfur dioxide, to the highest bidders.
Governments earn the most from spectrum auctions and quota auctions; Russia's crab quota sold for €2 billion in 2019.
The branch of economics that studies auction formats and how bidders behave is called auction theory.
Paul Milgrom and Robert B. Wilson won the 2020 Nobel Prize for introducing new auction formats.
Fishing quotas can be handed out for free or auctioned when a catch-share scheme starts.

definition.text: The main ways an auction's price can be set: open rising bids, a falling price called out by the auctioneer, or one-shot sealed bids.

facts.text: In an English auction bidders openly outbid one another, each bid higher than the last.
In a Dutch auction the auctioneer starts high and lowers the price until someone accepts it or the seller's reserve is reached.
In a first-price sealed-bid auction everyone submits one secret bid at the same time and the highest bidder pays what they bid.
A Vickrey (second-price sealed-bid) auction works the same way except that the winner pays the second-highest bid; it is central to auction theory and online ad bidding.

definition.text: A minimum price set by the seller below which the auctioned item will not be sold.

facts.text: In a no-reserve (absolute) auction the item sells whatever the price, which can draw more bidders hoping for a bargain.
A reserve protects the seller from a low bid but may lower the final price if it dampens interest.
The reserve can be announced to bidders (public) or kept secret.
Riley and Samuelson showed that discriminating against low-value buyers with a minimum price raises expected revenue.

title: Winner's curse

definition.text: The tendency of an auction winner who knows less about an item than the seller to overvalue it and overpay.

facts.text: Bid shading, bidding below one's true value for the item, is one way bidders guard against the winner's curse.
Bid shading risks losing the auction but may win the item cheaply.
When items go to whoever overvalues them most, resources may not end up with the person who values them most.
It arises in common-value settings, where actual values are unknown but correlated and bidders bid on estimated values.

notes: No page of its own here; drawn from Auction § Bidding strategy > By the bidders.

definition.text: Collusion in which bidders who know each other form a ring to avoid bidding against one another and so keep auction prices low.

facts.text: Ring members may hold their own private auction afterwards and split the price difference between the two sales.
Bid rigging weakens competition, discourages other bidders and denies the seller the item's true value.
Even without explicit agreement, bidders can in theory coordinate tacitly to keep bids low.

definition.text: A game-theory model of strategic decisions in which players have incomplete information, such as private knowledge of their own payoffs.

facts.text: John C. Harsanyi introduced Bayesian games in three papers in 1967 and 1968 and later shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
Nature assigns each player a 'type' at the start, standing for the private information that player holds.
Players hold a probability distribution over everyone's possible types; when no one has private information it is called a common prior.
Attaching probabilities to types lets games of incomplete information be solved for the first time, and far more easily than otherwise.
They avoid endless 'I think that you think' reasoning by weighting all possible outcomes by probability at once.
A buyer bidding for a used car whose quality only the owner knows, the market for lemons, is a Bayesian game linked to adverse selection.

definition.text: The Nash equilibrium of a Bayesian game, in which each player's strategy maximizes their expected payoff given their beliefs about others' types and the others' strategies.

facts.text: Players form their beliefs about the unknown state of nature using Bayes' rule.
In dynamic games where players move in turn, it can produce implausible equilibria based on non-credible strategies or beliefs.
In mechanism design, a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which everyone reports their true preferences makes a mechanism incentive compatible.

definition.text: An equilibrium of a sequential game with incomplete information in which beliefs are consistent with the strategies and every player chooses optimally given those beliefs.

facts.text: Like subgame perfect equilibrium, it requires play to be optimal from every information set onward, ruling out non-credible threats and beliefs.

definition.text: A group of a player's decision points that the player cannot tell apart, so they do not know which one they are at.

facts.text: In game trees information sets are usually drawn with dotted lines.
Chance moves are made by 'Nature', usually shown as an unfilled circle at the root of the tree.

definition.text: A two-player model of conflict, also called hawk–dove or snowdrift, in which each would like the other to back down but the worst outcome is that neither does.

facts.text: The name comes from two drivers heading at each other: one must swerve or both may die, and the one who swerves is called a 'chicken'.
Each driver does best by going straight while the other swerves, and a crash is the worst outcome for both.
Games of this anti-coordination type have three Nash equilibria: two where the players choose opposite actions and one mixed equilibrium where each randomizes.
The only symmetric equilibrium is the mixed one, which is often worse for both than if they could coordinate.
Where the prisoner's dilemma is about the impossibility of cooperation, Chicken is about the inevitability of conflict; repeated Chicken can lead to turn-taking.
'Schedule chicken' describes project teams each promising unrealistic dates because no one wants to be first to admit delay.

definition.text: The biologists' version of Chicken, in which two animals contest a shared resource and each can either fight (hawk) or back off (dove).

facts.text: John Maynard Smith and George Price first presented a form of it in their 1973 paper 'The logic of animal conflict'.
Payoffs depend on V, the value of the resource, and C, the cost of an escalated fight, and the cost is almost always assumed larger than the value.
It is the most commonly used game-theory model of aggression in biology, asking when an animal should escalate to costly combat.
If one player can be told apart as territory owner and the other as intruder, role-based pure strategies become evolutionarily stable instead of the mixed one.

definition.text: A tactic of convincingly locking in one's own choice before a game starts so that the other player must give way.

facts.text: A driver who visibly disables their steering wheel forces the other to swerve, showing that cutting one's own options can pay.
A protester who handcuffs themselves to an object is a real-world example: no threat can make them move.

definition.text: A simple model of how strategies spread in a population, used in evolutionary game theory.

facts.text: A strategy that does better than average grows in frequency at the expense of those doing worse than average.
One version has a single population playing against itself; another has two populations that each play only against the other.

definition.text: In game theory, a strategic move that deters an opponent from turning aggressive by credibly threatening a risk of irrational retaliation.

facts.text: The threat works only if the opponent believes there is enough risk of an irrational response, often because the threatener has given up control over it.
In everyday talk of conflict 'chicken' and 'brinkmanship' are often used as synonyms.

definition.text: A model of escalating conflict in which outcomes differ only by degree, as each side decides whether the prize is worth the mounting cost of carrying on.

facts.text: It differs from Chicken, where the catastrophic outcome differs in kind, such as life against death.
In biology it is a very influential model of how contests are settled when physical combat is not possible.

definition.text: A many-player game in which each person chooses whether to volunteer, doing best if someone else volunteers and worst if nobody does.

facts.text: It is one of the many-player games that reduce to Chicken, much as the public goods game reduces to a prisoner's dilemma with two players.
The more players there are, the more likely it is that no one volunteers.

definition.text: The problem of how two parties should split a surplus that they can only create together.

facts.text: Because the surplus can be divided many ways, the parties must negotiate; examples include firms and workers splitting profit, or trade partners setting terms of trade.
The normative approach sets out appealing rules (axioms) that a fair division should satisfy.
The positive approach studies how surpluses are actually shared, modelling bargaining as a non-cooperative game, most often sequential bargaining.
A bargaining problem consists of the set of feasible agreements and a disagreement point giving each player's payoff if no deal is reached.
Experiments found no consistent support for any bargaining model; many people settled on simple solutions good for both sides.
Kenneth Binmore used the Nash bargaining game and evolutionary game theory to explain why people see a 50–50 split as the just solution.

definition.text: The payoffs the bargaining parties can expect if negotiations break down.

facts.text: It might be a focal equilibrium both expect to play, or zero if no agreement is reached.
Since it shapes the final deal, each side gains by raising its own fallback payoff and lowering the other's, which is why it is also called the threat point.

definition.text: A simple two-player game in which each player demands a share of a good and both get their demands only if the total does not exceed what is available.

facts.text: It has many Nash equilibria: any pair of demands that exactly adds up to the whole is one.
Both players demanding everything is also an equilibrium, though both get nothing.
When uncertainty about feasible payoffs vanishes, its equilibrium payoffs converge to the Nash bargaining solution.

definition.text: A bargaining game in which the players take turns proposing how to split a surplus that shrinks with every round of delay.

facts.text: Its single subgame perfect equilibrium division depends on how strongly players prefer payoffs now over later.
With the surplus set to 1 and discount factor d, player 1 gets 1/(1+d) and player 2 gets d/(1+d).
As players become perfectly patient, the split converges to the Nash bargaining solution.

definition.text: A bargaining rule that replaces Nash's independence axiom with resource monotonicity and keeps the players' gains in the same ratio as their maximum possible gains.

facts.text: With the disagreement point at zero, it picks the efficient point whose payoffs stand in the ratio of each player's best achievable gain.

definition.text: A bargaining rule, introduced by Ehud Kalai, that gives both parties equal gains by maximizing the smaller of their payoffs.

facts.text: It drops scale invariance but keeps independence of irrelevant alternatives and resource monotonicity.
Kalai notes its closeness to the egalitarian ideas of John Rawls.

definition.text: The branch of game theory that studies games in which groups of players can form coalitions and make binding agreements, enforced from outside, for example by contract law.

facts.text: Non-cooperative games, by contrast, allow no alliances or only agreements that enforce themselves, such as through credible threats.
Analysis focuses on which coalitions can form, what they can do jointly and the collective payoffs that result.
The main assumption is that all players form one grand coalition; the question is then how to divide its total payoff among them.
Researchers have proposed different solution concepts, such as the core and the Shapley value, based on different ideas of fairness.
Cooperative game theory has been proposed as a strategic theory of the firm, with different solutions mimicking different institutions.

definition.text: In a cooperative game, the function that gives the total payoff each possible coalition of players can secure by joining together.

facts.text: A cooperative game is specified simply by giving a value for every coalition, with the empty coalition worth zero.
Characteristic functions are often assumed superadditive: two separate coalitions together are worth at least the sum of their separate values.
In a simple game every coalition is either winning (worth 1) or losing (worth 0).

definition.text: The von Neumann–Morgenstern solution: the first solution concept proposed for cooperative games with more than two players, built on which allocations a coalition would object to.

facts.text: One allocation dominates another if some coalition prefers it and could obtain at least its members' payoffs on its own.
A stable set may not exist, is usually not unique and is hard to find, which spurred the development of other solution concepts.
The core is contained in every stable set.

definition.text: The allocation of a cooperative game that makes the largest complaints of coalitions, measured by what each could gain by leaving, as small as possible.

facts.text: The nucleolus is always unique.
If the core is non-empty, the nucleolus lies inside it.

definition.text: The extra surplus a coalition creates beyond what its smaller sub-coalitions already create.

facts.text: John Harsanyi used it in 1963 to generalize the Shapley value.

definition.text: A cooperative game with a 'snowballing' property, formally a supermodular characteristic function, introduced by Shapley in 1971.

facts.text: Convex games are totally balanced: their core, and the core of every subgame, is non-empty.
Similar results for submodular functions appear in combinatorial optimization.

definition.text: A simultaneous game in which players earn more when they choose the same course of action as one another.

facts.text: It has several pure-strategy Nash equilibria in which players choose matching strategies, and each player's best move depends on what they expect the other to do.
Choosing which side of the road to drive on is the typical example: a shared standard that saves lives if widely followed.
When it does not matter which option is picked as long as both pick the same, it is a pure coordination game.
Coordination games also have a mixed equilibrium, but it is worse for both than either pure equilibrium and is not evolutionarily stable.
They are closely tied to positive network externalities, the benefit of being in the same network as others.
The stag hunt, or assurance game, is a coordination game where the best joint outcome needs trust, while a safer option needs none.

title: Battle of the sexes

definition.text: A coordination game with conflicting interests: both players prefer doing the same thing over going alone but disagree on which thing to do.

facts.text: The standard story is a couple arguing over what to do at the weekend.
A round of cheap talk before play may let the players pick one of its several equilibria and earn more than without communication.

notes: No page of its own crawled; defined in Coordination game § Examples and used on Cheap talk.

definition.text: A de facto standard that people adopt freely, the typical social-science solution to a coordination problem.

facts.text: Such standards tend to be stable where everyone gains, but only by making mutually consistent choices.
A standard enforced by law (a de jure obligation standard) is instead a solution to a prisoner's-dilemma-type problem.

definition.text: An equilibrium that people tend to settle on when they must coordinate without talking, because it stands out for some reason.

facts.text: An equilibrium may stand out by paying more, being more salient, fairer or safer.
These reasons can clash, as in the stag hunt, where hunting stag together pays more but hunting hare is safer.

definition.text: The common outcome in which players end up at a worse equilibrium because they pick the safer option instead of the one paying most.

facts.text: Players are more likely to fail to coordinate on the risky option when its extra reward over the safe option is small.
Laboratory results suggest coordination failure is common in stag-hunt and order-statistic games.
In one weak-link experiment groups first failed to coordinate, but about 80% coordinated successfully when the game was repeated.

definition.text: A game in which choosing the same action as others creates a cost rather than a benefit, as under negative externalities.

facts.text: Chicken (hawk–dove) is the best-known two-player example.
In a crowding game each player's payoff falls as more others choose the same strategy, as when extra cars slow a road for everyone; a congestion game is a crowding game in networks.
In a discoordination game one player wants to match and the other to mismatch, so the only equilibrium is mixed; matching pennies is the classic case.

definition.text: In a cooperative game, the set of allocations from which no group of players could do better by breaking away from the whole group.

facts.text: A coalition blocks an allocation if its members could create more value on their own than they are given.
The core corresponds to situations where cooperation among all players can be kept going.
The idea appeared in Edgeworth's 1881 writing as the contract curve; the modern definition is due to Donald B. Gillies and Lloyd Shapley.
The core is always well defined but can be empty; the Bondareva–Shapley theorem says it is non-empty exactly when the game is 'balanced'.
In a game of 1000 left-shoe and 1001 right-shoe owners, the core gives the scarce left-shoe owners everything and right-shoe owners nothing.
Critics note how extremely sensitive the core is to an oversupply of one type of player.
Every Walrasian (competitive market) equilibrium lies in the core, though not every core allocation is a market equilibrium.

title: Evolutionary game theory

definition.text: The use of game theory to study evolving populations of living things, modelling Darwinian competition as a contest between strategies.

facts.text: It began in 1973 with John Maynard Smith and George R. Price's formal treatment of animal contests as strategies.
Unlike classical game theory it does not need rational players, only inherited strategies whose success is tested by survival and reproduction.
It focuses on how strategies change over time, which depends on how common each competing strategy is in the population.
It has helped explain group selection, sexual selection, altruism, parental care, co-evolution and ecological dynamics.
It began from the puzzle of why animals fight in restrained, ritualized ways over resources.
Life's problems of getting food, surviving and reproducing resemble economic problems of resource management, competitive strategy and investment, which is why game theory fits biology so well.

distinct_from: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

title: Evolutionarily stable strategy
article: Evolutionary game theory#The evolutionarily stable strategy

definition.text: A strategy that, once common in a large population, cannot be invaded by any rare mutant strategy.

facts.text: It is akin to the Nash equilibrium of classical game theory, but with stricter mathematical conditions.
A successful strategy must be able to spread when rare and to hold its ground once common.
In the hawk–dove game the evolutionarily stable strategy is a mixed one.
The rock-paper-scissors game played by male side-blotched lizards has no evolutionarily stable strategy, only endless cycles around a Nash equilibrium.

distinct_from: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

title: Bourgeois strategy
article: Evolutionary game theory#Asymmetries that allow new strategies

definition.text: An evolutionary strategy that settles contests by using some asymmetry between the rivals, such as who already holds the resource.

facts.text: It can beat a bluffing strategy in the war of attrition when such an asymmetry exists.
In the hawk–dove game, treating one player as territory owner and the other as intruder makes role-based strategies stable.

distinct_from: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

title: Evolution of altruism

definition.text: The puzzle, noted by Darwin, of how behaviour that helps another at a cost to oneself can survive natural selection, and the game-theory routes that explain it.

facts.text: If selection acts only on individuals, altruism makes no sense, yet many social animals behave altruistically.
Kin selection explains it through shared genes; Hamilton's rule says relatedness must exceed the ratio of cost to benefit.
Direct reciprocity ('I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine') and indirect reciprocity are further routes.
Without some measure of reputation, only direct reciprocity can arise in the prisoner's dilemma.

contested_note: Nowak and Wilson's group-selection explanation of insect eusociality challenges the kin-selection account and is described as controversial.
distinct_from: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature
notes: Contested note rests on S:f92bb3cc7081 (Eusociality and kin selection).

title: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

definition.text: Evolutionary games in which each strategy beats one rival and loses to another, so the strategies' shares cycle instead of settling down.

facts.text: Male side-blotched lizards have three throat-colour types with different mating strategies that beat one another in a circle.
Together with density effects in females, this drives a four-year population cycle.
The cyclic behaviour predicted by evolutionary game theory has also been seen in human laboratory experiments.

title: Coevolutionary games

definition.text: Evolutionary game dynamics that combine competition within a species with competition between species.

facts.text: Examples include predator–prey competition, host–parasite co-evolution and mutualism.
They add a third kind of dynamic beyond games that settle at a stable strategy and games that cycle.

distinct_from: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

title: Spatial games

definition.text: Evolutionary game models that place players on a grid so that each contest is only with immediate neighbours.

facts.text: Winning strategies take over local neighbourhoods and then spread into adjacent ones.

distinct_from: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

definition.text: A way of describing a game as a tree that shows the order of moves, each player's choices at each point, what they know when they choose, and the payoffs at the end.

facts.text: It gives a fuller description than the normal form, which reduces a game to a payoff matrix.
Normal form is generally used for simultaneous games and extensive form for sequential ones; it is a many-player version of a decision tree.
Each end point (leaf) of the tree lists one payoff for every player, and a play is a path from the root to a leaf.
Chance events are modelled as moves by a fictitious player called Nature, whose branches carry probabilities.
Such games are solved by backward induction, working from the end nodes back to the root.
Harold W. Kuhn gave the general definition in 1953, extending one by von Neumann from 1928.

definition.text: A game has perfect information when every player always knows everything that has happened so far, and imperfect information when some earlier move is hidden.

facts.text: Moves may be unobserved because they are simultaneous or hidden.
A game with any information set of more than one node has imperfect information.
An information set is drawn as a dotted line or a loop joining the nodes the player cannot tell apart.

definition.text: The device of turning a game of incomplete information, where players do not know others' payoffs or types, into one of complete but imperfect information by letting Nature choose the types.

facts.text: For example, Nature might pick a job applicant's ability as low with probability 1/3 or high with probability 2/3, and the employer does not see the pick.
Nature has no payoffs and its choice is drawn as an unfilled node.

definition.text: A family of results showing that repeated games have a great many equilibrium outcomes: almost any payoff can be sustained if players are patient enough.

facts.text: It got its name because game theorists widely knew the result in the 1950s although nobody had published it.
'Almost any' means every payoff that is feasible and individually rational, that is, better than what each player can guarantee alone.
The simplest proof uses a grim trigger strategy: cooperate until someone deviates, then punish them forever.
Friedman's 1971 version strengthened it to subgame-perfect equilibria, where punishment threats must be credible.
It explains why agreements between countries are kept without enforcement: relations are long-term, though an impatient country is hard to punish credibly.
In a close-knit community it shows how traditions and taboos can be upheld by social norms.
Franklin Fisher noted it is not a positive theory: it does not predict what firms will do, only that cost and demand alone cannot explain oligopoly.

definition.text: A situation in a game where no player could do better by changing only their own strategy while everyone else keeps theirs.

facts.text: It is used to analyse any strategic interaction, where each decision-maker's outcome depends on the others' choices as well as their own.
Nash's insight was that the choices of several decision-makers cannot be predicted by analysing each one in isolation.
It is named after John Forbes Nash Jr., but Antoine Augustin Cournot used the same idea in 1838 for firms choosing how much to produce.
A Nash equilibrium need not be Pareto optimal, so it can look irrational from outside: everyone could be better off.
In sequential games it can rest on threats players would never carry out; subgame perfect equilibrium removes these.
It is applied to predict traffic flows, where each traveller's route time depends on the routes everyone else picks.
John Maynard Smith applied the concept to model the evolution of behaviour in 1982.

definition.text: A Nash equilibrium in which at least one player randomizes, choosing among strategies with set probabilities rather than always playing the same one.

facts.text: In the drive-on-the-left-or-right game, besides the two pure equilibria there is a third where each side is chosen with 50% probability.
In matching pennies, where one player wins on a match and the other on a mismatch, the only equilibrium is mixed.
An equilibrium is strict if every player would lose by switching, and weak if some player is indifferent.

definition.text: A refinement of Nash equilibrium that is stable against deviations by any coalition of players, not just by single players.

facts.text: Ordinary Nash equilibrium counts only individual deviations, which is not convincing enough for cooperative games.

definition.text: Nash's theorem that every game with finitely many players and finitely many pure strategies has at least one Nash equilibrium once mixed strategies are allowed.

facts.text: Equilibria may fail to exist when choices are infinite and unbounded, as when two players name numbers and the larger wins.
Nash's thesis proof used Brouwer's fixed-point theorem; his 1950 paper used the simpler Kakutani fixed-point theorem.
Robert Wilson's 1971 oddness theorem says almost all finite games have a finite, odd number of Nash equilibria.

definition.text: A description of a game as a table (payoff matrix) listing each player's possible strategies and the payoffs for every combination of them.

facts.text: Each cell gives the row player's payoff first and the column player's second.
It suits games where players move at the same time or cannot see each other's move first.
It makes dominated strategies and Nash equilibria easy to spot, but loses some information compared with the extensive form.
In the prisoner's dilemma matrix, Defect beats Cooperate whatever the other does, so (Defect, Defect) is the only Nash equilibrium.
A sequential game can be written in normal form only by listing every contingent plan, including for situations that never arise.
Every extensive-form game has an equivalent normal form, though converting can make the representation exponentially larger.

definition.text: A game made of the same base game (the stage game) played over and over by the same players.

facts.text: Repetition makes players weigh how today's action affects others' future actions, an effect sometimes called reputation.
Two neighbouring petrol stations would both earn zero profit in a one-off price war, yet they make profits because they meet again every day.
Repeating the same game a finite or an infinite number of times can lead to very different equilibria and best strategies.
In the infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma the preferred strategy is to cooperate rather than play the one-shot Nash strategy.
Sustaining cooperation relies on punishing anyone who deviates; results showing which outcomes can be sustained are the folk theorems.
A game repeated an unknown number of times is treated like an infinitely repeated one, since there is no known last round.

definition.text: A repeated-game strategy that cooperates until the other player deviates and then punishes them with play that lowers both players' payoffs.

facts.text: Knowing the other follows a trigger strategy, a player expects lower future payoffs if they act selfishly now.
An effective trigger makes cooperating worth more than grabbing a gain now and suffering punishment later.
The harshest form, grim trigger, punishes forever and is used to prove the folk theorem.

definition.text: A repeated game played for a fixed, known number of rounds, with each player's total payoff the sum over all rounds.

facts.text: If the stage game has a single Nash equilibrium, players play it in every round: reasoning backward from the last round unravels any cooperation.
A known, finite end therefore undermines cooperation in every round; cooperation is possible only when the number of rounds is infinite or unknown.
If the stage game has several equilibria, the threat of switching to a worse one later can support cooperation in earlier rounds.

definition.text: A method of fairly dividing the total gains or costs of a group effort among its members according to each one's average contribution.

facts.text: It looks at how much the result changes when a player joins every possible combination of others, then averages those changes.
Lloyd Shapley introduced it in 1951.
It is the only division satisfying efficiency, symmetry, additivity and the null-player property, widely accepted as defining fairness.
Efficiency means all the group's gain is shared out; a player who adds nothing to any coalition gets zero.
If cooperation creates positive synergy, every member gains at least what they could get alone.
It is used to divide business profits and to measure each feature's importance in machine-learning models and sensitivity analysis.

definition.text: An extension of the Shapley value to games with a continuum of players, each of whom plays only a tiny role.

facts.text: Lloyd Shapley and Robert Aumann created it in their 1974 book; Jean-François Mertens and Abraham Neyman extended it further.

definition.text: A game, also called the assurance game or trust dilemma, in which players do best by cooperating on an ambitious goal but can fall back on a safer solo option that protects them if the other does not cooperate.

facts.text: Two hunters choose separately whether to hunt a stag, which needs both of them, or a hare, which one can catch alone but is worth far less.
It has two pure equilibria: hunting stag together pays most, while hunting hare alone is the safer, risk-dominant choice.
Unlike the prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is itself an equilibrium; what it needs is trust.
It is often used as an analogy for social cooperation such as international agreements on climate change.
The problem originated with Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality; David Hume gave examples such as two neighbours draining a meadow.
Orcas that cooperatively herd fish to the surface, which needs many orcas, are an animal example.
Expected punishment of defectors can turn a prisoner's dilemma into a stag hunt.

definition.text: One strategy dominates another if it always gives a better result, whatever the other players do.

facts.text: Strict dominance means always strictly better; weak dominance means never worse and sometimes better.
A strategy that dominates every alternative is a dominant strategy; rational players are usually assumed never to play dominated strategies.
If every player has a strictly dominant strategy, the game has a single dominant-strategy equilibrium, which need not be good for everyone.
The prisoner's dilemma is the classic case: confessing dominates for each suspect although both would do better staying silent.
Strictly dominated strategies are never part of a Nash equilibrium, but weakly dominated ones can be.

title: Iterated elimination of dominated strategies
article: Strategic dominance#Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies

definition.text: A way of solving games by repeatedly crossing out dominated strategies until no more can be removed.

facts.text: Removing some strategies can make others dominated in the smaller game, so the step is repeated.
It relies on rationality being common knowledge: everyone knows that everyone knows, and so on, that all players are rational.
With weakly dominated strategies the result can depend on the order in which they are removed.

definition.text: A player's complete plan for a game, saying what they will do in every situation that might arise.

facts.text: A move or action is any one of the options a player can choose where the best result depends on what others do as well.
A strategy is like a list of directions, and a move is a single step on that list.
A player's strategy set lists every strategy available to them, such as {rock, paper, scissors}.
In games played over time or with private information, strategies are rules for how to respond to each possible history or piece of information.
Choosing the strategy sets well is part of the art of making an applied game both solvable and meaningful.

definition.text: A strategy in which the player chooses among their pure strategies at random with set probabilities, rather than committing to one plan.

facts.text: A pure strategy is a fully fixed plan; it counts as a mixed strategy that picks one option with probability 1.
Mixing helps where no pure strategy is a best response, keeping a player unpredictable; payoffs are then expected payoffs.
A soccer penalty kick has no pure-strategy equilibrium, so kicker and goalie should both randomize their direction.
Not every finite game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, as matching pennies shows, but every one has an equilibrium once mixing is allowed.

Critics in the 1980s found mixed strategies intuitively problematic; Harsanyi's purification reads them as our ignorance of players' private information, and another view treats them as shares of a population.

definition.text: A strategy that randomizes separately at each information set over the actions available there, rather than over whole plans.

facts.text: A mixed strategy randomly picks a fixed path through the game tree, while a behavior strategy takes a random path.
Kuhn's theorem shows the two are equivalent in finite extensive-form games with perfect recall, where players remember all past actions.
The Absent-Minded Driver game shows why perfect recall is needed for this equivalence.

definition.text: A refinement of Nash equilibrium for games with moves in sequence, requiring the strategies to form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, from any point onward.

facts.text: It rules out non-credible threats, so strategies stay rational throughout the game.
Reinhard Selten proposed it in 1965.
Every finite game with complete information and perfect recall has one.
In finite games it is usually found by backward induction, though that does not work for infinite or imperfect-information games.
The ultimatum game is a classic example with fewer subgame perfect equilibria than Nash equilibria.
In a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, backward induction makes both players defect in every round.
Firms in repeated Cournot competition can collude on the monopoly outcome in a subgame perfect equilibrium if they are patient enough.

title: Backward induction

definition.text: Solving a sequential game by starting from the last move, working out what the final mover would do, and reasoning back to the start.

facts.text: At each step it removes branches where a player would make a move that is not in their interest at that point.
Tic-tac-toe has a well-known backward-induction solution, and in theory even Go has one.
Finite repeated games can be solved this way, but games repeated forever or an unknown number of times cannot, as there is no last round.
Kaminski (2019) proved that a generalized backward induction finds all subgame perfect equilibria in a broad class of games.

notes: No page of its own crawled; anchored to the SPE section that explains it.

title: Credible threat

definition.text: A threat a player would actually want to carry out if the time came; a non-credible threat is one that would hurt the player making it.

facts.text: Plain Nash equilibrium can rest on threats players would never carry out; subgame perfection eliminates them.
In Chicken, a player who rips out their steering wheel always wins, because the opponent's threat to crash anyway is not credible.
If punishing a deviator is costly to the punishers, the threat of punishment is not credible.

notes: No page of its own; discussed on Subgame perfect equilibrium, Nash equilibrium, Folk theorem and Cooperative game theory.

definition.text: A repeated-game strategy that cooperates on the first move and then copies whatever the opponent did on the previous move.

facts.text: The phrase means 'equivalent retaliation' and was first recorded in 1558.
Anatol Rapoport entered it in Robert Axelrod's two tournaments around 1980, where it was both the simplest strategy and the most successful.
Its success may help explain how animal and human groups came to live in mostly cooperative ways.
A single misread move can trap two tit-for-tat players in an endless 'death spiral' of alternating retaliation.
It is not a subgame perfect equilibrium except under knife-edge conditions on the discount rate.
In First World War trenches it appeared as the 'live and let live' system, an unspoken truce kept by matching retaliation.
In repeated social dilemmas, cooperation may emerge when people adopt tit for tat.

title: Tit for two tats
article: Tit for tat#Tit for two tats

definition.text: A more forgiving version of tit for tat that retaliates only after the opponent defects twice in a row.

facts.text: Letting a single defection pass avoids the 'death spiral' of two retaliators punishing each other forever.
Robert Axelrod found it would have outscored every program in his first tournament.
BitTorrent file-sharing peers use a variant of it to swap upload for download bandwidth.

title: Generous tit for tat
article: Tit for tat#Generous tit for tat

definition.text: A version of tit for tat that, after the opponent defects, usually retaliates but sometimes cooperates anyway, with a small probability.

facts.text: Occasional forgiveness breaks cycles of retaliation caused by mistakes or 'noise' and restores mutual cooperation.
Axelrod found it highly effective in noisy settings; the forgiveness probability can be around 1–5%, depending on the opponents.

title: Reciprocal altruism
article: Tit for tat#Explaining reciprocal altruism in animal communities

definition.text: Helping another animal in the expectation that the favour will be returned when needs reverse, explained by tit-for-tat strategies.

facts.text: It works where the cost to the helper of sharing food, mates, nests or territory is less than the gain to the one helped.
Ways of spotting and punishing 'cheaters' who fail to return favours, in effect tit for tat, keep it stable.
Tit for tat has been suggested as the mechanism behind guppies' cooperative inspection of predators.

title: Axelrod's tournaments
article: Prisoner's dilemma#Axelrod's tournament and successful strategy conditions

definition.text: Computer tournaments organized by Robert Axelrod in which strategies submitted by academics competed in the repeated prisoner's dilemma.

facts.text: Greedy strategies did poorly over the long run, and the simple tit for tat won.
Axelrod concluded that successful strategies are nice, retaliating, forgiving and non-envious.
He used the results to show how altruism could evolve by natural selection from purely selfish beginnings, reported in his 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation.

definition.text: A situation in which one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss, so gains and losses add up to zero.

facts.text: Cutting a cake is zero-sum if everyone values each piece equally: a bigger slice for one leaves less for others.
Poker, chess, sport and bridge are everyday examples; in finance, futures, options and swaps are zero-sum.
Such games are distributive: the pie cannot be enlarged by good negotiation, only divided.
Every two-player finite zero-sum game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies, and there Nash equilibrium, minimax and maximin all give the same answer.
The solution of a two-player zero-sum game can be found by solving a linear programming problem.
In 1944 von Neumann and Morgenstern showed any non-zero-sum game of n players equals a zero-sum game with an extra fictitious player.

definition.text: A situation in which one party's gain need not be another's loss, so the total of gains and losses can be more or less than zero.

facts.text: Positive-sum or win–win games are those where the parties' combined gains exceed zero.
Two countries swapping surplus bananas for surplus apples, both benefiting, is a non-zero-sum situation.
The prisoner's dilemma is a classic non-zero-sum game.
Politics and the economy need not be zero-sum because of cooperation, synergy and economic growth.

definition.text: The belief that a situation is zero-sum, so that one person's gain must be another's loss, summed up as 'your gain is my loss'.

facts.text: Unlike the game-theory concept, it is a psychological construct: a person's subjective reading of a situation.
Applying zero-sum logic where it does not fit can breed needless feelings of scarcity and hostility.
Economic stagnation can encourage zero-sum perceptions, which can raise support for redistribution.

definition.text: Knowledge shared by a group such that everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on without end.

facts.text: David Lewis introduced the idea in philosophy in his 1969 study Convention; Robert Aumann gave it a mathematical, set-theoretic form in 1976.
A trustworthy public announcement makes a fact common knowledge, but telling each agent privately yields only mutual knowledge.
The blue-eyed islanders puzzle shows its force: after a public announcement that at least one has blue eyes, all k blue-eyed people leave on the kth dawn.

title: Kin selection

definition.text: A process in which natural selection favours a trait because it helps the reproductive success of an organism's relatives, even at a cost to the organism itself.

facts.text: It can lead to altruistic behaviour and is tied to inclusive fitness, which counts offspring produced and those an individual helps produce, weighted by relatedness.
Hamilton's 1964 rule says a behaviour spreads when relatedness times benefit to the recipient exceeds the cost to the actor.
Altruism can be favoured by kin recognition or in 'viscous' populations with limited dispersal, where neighbours are usually relatives.
Humans favour kin, for example in wills in proportion to relatedness, though many evolutionary psychologists warn that relatedness is not the same as shared genes.

contested_note: Critics such as Alonso and Wilson, Nowak and Tarnita dispute inclusive fitness theory.

definition.text: A pattern in which a population rises and falls over a predictable period.

facts.text: Food supply, predators, disease and climate all influence population change, yet the full cause of cycles is a major unsolved ecological problem.
Snowshoe hare catches in Hudson's Bay Company records ran in a cycle of about ten years.
Predators track prey: more prey means more food for predators, and when prey declines predator numbers come under pressure.

definition.text: A condition on roads marked by slower speeds, longer trip times and more vehicle queuing.

facts.text: Congestion occurs when traffic demands more space than street capacity provides, a point called saturation.
It can be seen as a tragedy of the commons: roads are usually free at the point of use, so drivers have little incentive to hold back until demand is limited by opportunity cost.
Adding road capacity tends to attract more traffic (induced demand), and Braess's paradox shows extra capacity can worsen congestion even without more demand.

definition.text: The motivation to answer kind behavior with kindness and unfair behavior with unkindness.

facts.text: In social psychology reciprocity is a learned norm of answering an action with an equivalent one, rewarding positive actions and punishing negative ones.
Fehr and Gächter's public goods experiments showed people in reciprocal settings deviate from pure self-interest more than in other contexts.
Reciprocity often exceeds what rational self-interest predicts and tends to win out over it in competitive markets with incomplete contracts.
Positive reciprocity returns a favour with one of roughly equal positive value.
